question: Czech and Belgian authorities have revealed that Members of the European Parliament, among others, have been approached and even paid to promote Russian propaganda. The news outlet ‘Voice of Europe’ features prominently in these severe allegations of Russian interference.

While it is up to the relevant public prosecutor’s offices to take judicial action in the face of such allegations, justifiable worries exist that this kind of corruption is linked to various political parties, in several Member States, that are participating in the upcoming European elections. 1.

Which further measures will the Commission take to protect the June 2024 European elections in order to prevent interference by autocratic regimes in our democratic process, and how will the Commission restore public trust in the European elections and in the integrity of politicians?

Is the Commission considering reviewing the regulation on the statute and funding of European political parties1 to ensure that the financing of political parties and candidates happens with integrity and in a transparent way, also considering the June 2024 European elections?

How can the Commission help parliamentarians arm themselves against foreign information manipulation and interference, and will the Commission make a plan to prevent candidates who receive support in exchange for promoting dubious propaganda from entering the institutions, for example through the StratCom Task Force but also through other networks?

Regulation (EU, Euratom) No 1141/2014 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 22 October 2014 on the statute and funding of European political parties and European political foundations (OJ L 317, 4.11.2014, p. 1).
answer: The Commission adopted in December 2023, as part of the Defence of Democracy package (1), a recommendation on inclusive and resilient elections (2), which calls on political parties to assess risks stemming from donations from third countries and donations potentially linked to criminal activity.

Following up on the recommendation, all European political parties signed a code of conduct in which they commit to, among others, avoid amplification of narratives lead by entities and actors from outside the EU other than member parties, especially when those seek to erode European values.

Pursuant to its Article 38, both Commission (3) and Parliament (4) evaluated Regulation 1141/2014 (5) in 2021 with overall positive findings. Both institutions however identified a number of shortcomings. The Commission thus adopted on 25 November 2021 a proposal to recast the regulation (6).

The co-legislators could not find an interinstitutional agreement on the file before the elections to the European Parliament. The Commission is ready to follow up on discussions in the new parliamentary term. The EU has built significant expertise in detecting, analysing and countering foreign information manipulation and interference.

The EU and its Member States have developed the Foreign Information Manipulation and Interference (FIMI) toolbox, which outlines options to tackle the threat from the EU level. Protecting the integrity of elections is also a priority in the Commission’s enforcement of the Digital Services Ac t (7), as demonstrated by the several non-compliance cases that it has already opened.
